full_judgment: 8. It is unnecessary to notice the history of the section which were enacted in 1929. It will be sufficient to note that the contract must be in writing as section itself opens up by saying where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immovable property by writing signed by him." The first requisite is the contract is to be written one unlike England where the Parol contract is admissible and by virtue of this section part performance does not give rise to an equity as in England but to a statutory right as given in section 53A. This right is more restricted than the English equity in two respects; (a) there must be a written contract and (2) it is only available as a defence. A formal lease is not necessary to attract the application of section 53A. All that is required is that an agreement in writing signed by the transferor. In Maniklal Mansukhbhasi Vs. Hormanji Jamshedji Ginwalla & Sons, A.I.R. 1950 (SC) page 1 in an action to eject a lessee on the, ground that he had no registered deed of lease in his favour, the defendant lessee took the plea of part performance and proved that there was a written and signed contract in his favour and that he had taken possession in accordance with the terms of the agreement and he was paying rent to the plaintiff in accordance with the agreement. It was held that the defendant is entitled to retain possession in spite of absence of the registered deed. This is the relief that has been given by section 53A which is of doctrine of English part performance but the conditions precedent for attracting the section is the written agreement which in the present case is not to be found nor the defendant himself claimed that he had any written contract. His sole case was that it was an oral contract. In case of Krishna Sardar Vs. Sindhu Bala Dasi A.I.R. 1970 Cal. 444 the plea of part performance was not available to the defendant when the defendant placed before the Court the Memorandum of recording fact of taking possession under agreement of exchange. It was held that such Memorandum is not a contract or deed of exchange which along on registration can pass title to the parties concerned. The Court observed that the whole controversy between the parties rest on the fact of a memorandum on the rights of the parties under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. The Court held that section 53A has no manner of application as it refers to a contract in writing which a memorandum is not In obis view of the matter there is no hesitation in saying that the learned Single Judge was correct in setting aside the judgment and decree of the courts below though the discussion is not to be found on section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. The learned Single Judge was correct that the defendant was not better than a licensee and the appeal was correctly allowed in accordance with law.
